settings.label: How MUTO is built for it
What changes after 35
settings.heading: Somewhere after 35, your body starts working a little differently.
settings.intro: Nothing dramatic happens overnight. But three quiet shifts start inside your cells, and they build through your 40s and 50s.
settings.takeaway: It’s not you doing anything wrong. It’s biology. And what your body needs changes with it.

settings.title: You make less NAD+
settings.text: A molecule every cell needs to turn food into energy.

settings.title: You get less back
settings.text: From the same food and the same training.

settings.title: Your cells’ maintenance slows
settings.text: While the wear and tear of making energy carries on.

settings.label: How it shows up
settings.heading: You don’t feel your cells. You feel your day.
settings.intro: This is what people in their late 30s, 40s and 50s tell us, again and again:
settings.line: It’s like your body has switched to low power mode. Still working, still getting through the day, but running on less than it used to.

settings.text: The same training just doesn’t land like it used to.
Hard sessions hang around for days.
I spend Saturdays recovering from the week.
There’s nothing left for the people at home.
I’m doing everything right, and I still feel it.

settings.label: The science behind it
settings.heading: What’s actually happening inside you.
settings.takeaway: Three shifts, one root: what your cells need changes, and the basics you took at 30 weren’t built for it.

settings.title: 30 trillion tiny factories
settings.text: Every cell makes its own energy, in tiny power stations called mitochondria.

settings.title: Fewer couriers
settings.text: To make that energy, cells use NAD+ as a courier: it picks up energy from your food and carries it to the power station, over and over, all day. From your mid-30s, your body makes less NAD+. Fewer couriers, the same amount of work.

settings.title: Less back from the same input
settings.text: As we age, our bodies respond less to the same food and the same training. It’s called anabolic resistance, and it’s what I spent years studying in the lab. Same effort, smaller return.

settings.title: More wear, slower maintenance
settings.text: Making energy creates a little “exhaust”. Your cells have crews that clean it up and keep everything maintained, and some of those crews, a family of enzymes called sirtuins, also use NAD+ every time they work. Fewer couriers means more competition for the same supply.

settings.heading: How the 19 ingredients work together
settings.rows:
Team | Who’s on it | What happens
The energy team | NR, CoQ10, copper | NR becomes NAD+, the courier. CoQ10 is the relay runner that passes energy along inside the power station. Copper sits at the very last step, where the energy gets made.
The recycling team | Folate, B12, B6, TMG | Your cells constantly reuse one of their most important building blocks. Folate and B12 keep that recycling loop turning, TMG runs a second loop alongside it, and B6 handles the exit. We use the active forms, the ones the cell actually uses.
The clean-up crew | Zinc + copper | Zinc and copper build the enzyme that cleans up the exhaust from making energy. One enzyme, two metals, so we pair them.
The bone relay | D3 + K2 | D3 tells your cells to make a bone protein. K2 switches that protein on. D3 makes it, K2 activates it.
